accordingly: shows that something is done in a way that fits the situation or what has just been said
typical: at the end of a clause, formal or neutral, e.g. act accordingly, adjust accordingly. NOT for: introducing a result at the start of a sentence (see the other function).
Please check the new rules and act accordingly.
If the weather changes, we will adjust the plan accordingly.
He was a guest, so we treated him accordingly.
introduces something that happens because of what has just been said
typical: formal writing, at the start of a sentence or after a comma. NOT for: casual speech, where 'so' is more natural.
The old rules were unclear. Accordingly, the committee wrote new ones.
Demand fell sharply; accordingly, the company reduced its prices.
The data was incomplete. Accordingly, the study was repeated.
act out: perform a story or situation with actions, like a short play
typical: act out a scene, act sth out; role-play and drama lessons. NOT for: pretending in order to trick someone.
The children acted out the story of the three bears.
In class we acted the dialogue out in pairs.
show strong feelings through bad behaviour instead of talking about them
typical: act out at school; children and teenagers. NOT for: performing in a play.
After the move, the little boy began to act out at school.
Some teenagers act out when they feel nobody listens to them.
add up: find the total of several numbers or amounts
typical: add up the bill, add sth up. NOT for: putting one more thing with others (use add).
Let's add up how much we spent on the trip.
He added the figures up twice to be sure.
typical: usually negative, e.g. it doesn't add up. NOT for: calculating a total.
His explanation just doesn't add up.
The facts add up: someone inside the company helped.
typical: small savings/costs add up, add up to sth. NOT for: giving the exact total of a bill.
Small savings add up over the years.
Those short calls really add up on the phone bill.
admittedly: admits that something is true, even though it goes against your main point
typical: neutral to formal, at the start of a sentence or in the middle. NOT for: apologising or confessing a mistake (use 'I admit').
The hotel was admittedly a bit noisy, but the staff were wonderful.
Admittedly, I haven't read the whole report, but I've seen the main figures.
She is, admittedly, not the most experienced candidate.
after that: shows what happens next, after the event you have just mentioned
typical: telling a story or steps, e.g. We ate. After that, we left. NOT for: two things happening at the same time.
We watched the film. After that, we went for pizza.
He studied until six. After that, he was too tired to cook.
First she checked the map; after that, she started the car.
afterwards: shows that something happens after the event or time you have just mentioned
typical: at the end of a clause or at the start of a sentence, spoken and written (AmE also 'afterward'). NOT for: use before a noun (use 'after') or for 'at some later time from now' (use 'later').
We had dinner and went for a walk afterwards.
The lecture was boring. Afterwards, we all went for coffee.
Call me afterwards and tell me how it went.
agree with: have the same opinion as someone
typical: agree with sb/an idea. NOT for: saying yes to a plan or request (use agree to).
Most people agree with the new rule.
be good for your body, usually about food or climate
typical: usually negative, e.g. the fish didn't agree with me. NOT for: having the same opinion.
Spicy food doesn't agree with me.
The hot climate never agreed with her.
match in grammar or in facts
typical: a verb agrees with its subject; two reports agree with each other. NOT for: people sharing an opinion.
In English, the verb must agree with the subject.
His story agrees with what the witness said.
all the same: says that something is still true or still done in spite of what you have just said
typical: spoken and written, at the start of a sentence or at the end of a clause, often after 'but'. NOT for: 'exactly the same' or 'all of one kind'.
I know it's expensive, but I'm buying it all the same.
The forecast was bad. All the same, we decided to go ahead with the picnic.
She disagreed with him, but she listened to him all the same.
all things considered: gives your final opinion after thinking about all the points
typical: at the start or end of a sentence, neutral. NOT for: judging after looking at only one factor.
All things considered, the trip was a success.
It rained twice, but all things considered, we had a good holiday.
All things considered, I think we should wait until spring.
also: adds another fact or idea to what you have said
typical: before the main verb or after 'be', e.g. She also speaks French. NOT for: showing contrast; at the end of a sentence use 'too' or 'as well'.
The hotel is cheap, and it is also very clean.
starts a sentence to add one more point
typical: spoken, e.g. Also, it's cheaper. NOT for: written English, where it is better to use 'furthermore' or 'moreover' or to put 'also' before the main verb.
Also, the train is cheaper than the bus.
Also, don't forget to lock the door.
Also, we should check the opening hours.
alternatively: offers a different possibility that could be chosen instead
typical: neutral to formal, at the start of a sentence or after a semicolon. NOT for: adding a point (use 'also') or showing contrast (use 'however').
You can take the train; alternatively, you can go by bus.
We could meet at the café; alternatively, we could just talk online.
Add a little water. Alternatively, use milk for a creamier sauce.
and: addition
joins words, phrases or ideas that belong together
typical: tea and toast, tired and hungry, two similar ideas in one sentence. NOT for: showing contrast (use 'but') or a choice (use 'or').
I packed a sandwich and an apple for the trip.
The room was quiet and very warm.
We talked about the plan and about the costs.
sequence
shows that one action happens after another
typical: telling a story or giving steps, e.g. grab your bag and go. NOT for: actions that happen at the same time or in no fixed order.
She picked up her bag and walked out.
He read the note and put it in his pocket.
Open the app and tap the green button.
result
shows that the second thing happens because of the first
typical: informal storytelling, e.g. forgot my keys and got locked out. NOT for: giving a reason before the result (use 'because').
I stayed up too late and overslept this morning.
He ignored the warning and burned his hand.
She skipped breakfast and felt dizzy by ten.
new point
starts a sentence in speech to introduce a new statement, comment or question
typical: spoken, e.g. And what about you? NOT for: formal writing, where starting a sentence with 'and' is usually avoided.
And what did she say when you told her?
And one more thing: please bring your ID.
And who is going to pay for all this?
prompting
asks the other person to say more after they have just told you something
typical: spoken, as a short reply, e.g. And? NOT for: asking a yes/no question or continuing your own sentence.
'I called your office today.' 'And?' 'They said you were out.'
'We found the place.' 'And? Was it open?'
'She said yes.' 'And?' 'And she'll start in May.'
answer back: reply rudely to someone who has authority over you
typical: children answering back to parents or teachers. NOT for: giving a polite reply (use answer).
Don't answer back when your mother is talking to you.
He was sent out of class for answering the teacher back.
apply for: make a formal request for a job, place, visa or permit
typical: apply for a job/a loan/a visa. NOT for: using a rule or idea in practice (use apply to).
She applied for a job at the museum.
You must apply for a visa before you travel.
arrive at: reach a place at the end of a journey
typical: arrive at a station/airport/hotel; for a town or country use arrive in. NOT for: reaching a decision.
We arrived at the hotel just before midnight.
The train arrives at platform four at noon.
reach a decision, answer or agreement after thinking
typical: arrive at a decision/a conclusion/a figure. NOT for: reaching a place.
After long talks, they arrived at a compromise.
How did you arrive at that number?
as a result: shows that what follows happens because of what you have just said
typical: at the start of a sentence or after a comma, mostly in writing and careful speech. NOT for: giving the cause (use 'because').
The road was closed. As a result, many people were late for work.
She practised every day and, as a result, her English improved quickly.
Prices went up last year. As a result, fewer people bought new cars.
gives the cause of something when it is followed by 'of' and a noun
typical: as a result of + noun, e.g. as a result of the storm. NOT for: introducing a new sentence about a result (use 'as a result,').
Many flights were cancelled as a result of the storm.
As a result of the new law, smoking is banned here.
He lost his job as a result of the merger.
as far as ... is concerned: shows whose opinion you are giving, or whom something affects
typical: spoken, e.g. As far as I'm concerned, ... NOT for: facts that are true for everyone.
As far as I'm concerned, the case is closed.
As far as my sister is concerned, holidays mean beaches.
As far as the neighbours are concerned, the noise is a real problem.
says which subject you are talking about before you comment on it
typical: spoken and written, followed by a comment, also 'where ... is concerned'. NOT for: giving someone's opinion.
As far as money is concerned, we're fine for now.
As far as the schedule is concerned, nothing has changed.
As far as food is concerned, the hotel has a lot to offer.
ask around: ask several different people for information or help
typical: informal, e.g. I'll ask around. NOT for: asking only one person.
I'll ask around and see if anyone has a spare ticket.
She asked around the office, but nobody had seen the keys.
ask for: say that you want something to be given to you
typical: ask for help/advice/the bill. NOT for: asking a question to get information (use ask).
She asked for a glass of water.
Don't be afraid to ask for help.
say that you want to speak to a particular person
typical: ask for the manager, ask for sb at reception. NOT for: asking a person a question.
When you arrive, ask for Mrs Novak at reception.
He phoned the office and asked for the manager.
behave in a way that is likely to cause trouble for yourself
typical: informal, ask for trouble, be asking for it. NOT for: politely requesting something.
Driving that fast in the rain is asking for trouble.
If you leave your bag there, you're asking for it.
ask out: invite someone to go on a date
typical: ask sb out, e.g. he asked her out. NOT for: inviting someone to a group event.
He finally asked her out after three months.
I was too shy to ask him out.
at first: describes how things were at the beginning, before they changed
typical: At first..., but later/now... NOT for: the first step in a list (use 'first') or something that finally happens (use 'at last').
At first, I couldn't understand the accent, but now it's easy.
At first the water felt very cold.
I didn't like her at first, but we became good friends.
